title: A commutative algebraic group has a common eigenline in every nonzero rational module
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G$ be an affine group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space and $r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ a homomorphism of group schemes, where $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is the general linear group [def-sc-general-linear-group] after choosing a basis. A subspace $W\subseteq V$ is $G$-stable if $r_A(g)(A\otimes_kW)\subseteq A\otimes_kW$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and $g\in G(A)$. A character is a group-scheme homomorphism $\chi:G\to\mathbf G_m$, with $\mathbf G_m=\operatorname{GL}_1$. Assume that $G$ is commutative, meaning that its multiplication is unchanged by interchanging the factors. If $V\ne0$, then $V$ has a one-dimensional $G$-stable subspace $L$. Its restricted action is a character: there exists $\chi:G\to\mathbf G_m$ such that $r_A(g)(1\otimes v)=\chi_A(g)(1\otimes v)$ for every $A,g$ and $v\in L$. No smoothness or connectedness hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Corollary 16.14, printed p.329, together with Definition 16.1, printed p.324; one-dimensional subrepresentation is the definition of an eigenvector there.

proof.text: Choose a basis of $V$, and put $B=k[G]$. By affine-spectrum functoriality [def-weil-affine-spectrum] and the point description of [def-sc-general-linear-group], the universal point $u\in G(B)$ corresponds to $1_B$, and its image is an invertible matrix $R=(b_{ab})$ over $B$. For $g\in G(A)$ corresponding to $f_g:B\to A$, naturality says $r_A(g)=(f_g(b_{ab}))$. Take a basis $c_1,\ldots,c_m$ of the finite-dimensional $k$-span of the finitely many entries $b_{ab}$. Write $b_{ab}=\sum_i t_{i,ab}c_i$ with $t_{i,ab}\in k$, and let $T_i=(t_{i,ab})$. Thus $R=\sum_i c_iT_i$ and $r_A(g)=\sum_i f_g(c_i)(T_i)_A$. This is a finite matrix expansion, with no density argument.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, universal point and matrix coefficients; explicit finite coefficient expansion.

proof.text: Form the commutative $k$-algebra $C=B\otimes_kB$ using [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property](1). The maps $b\mapsto b\otimes1$ and $b\mapsto1\otimes b$ give points $u_1,u_2\in G(C)$. Commutativity of $G$ [def-sc-group-scheme] implies $u_1u_2=u_2u_1$, so their representation matrices commute. Expanding gives $\sum_{i,j}(c_i\otimes c_j)(T_iT_j-T_jT_i)=0$. Extend the linearly independent $c_i$ to a $k$-basis of $B$, and let $\ell_i:B\to k$ be its coordinate maps. For every matrix entry apply the linear map $B\otimes_kB\to k$, $b\otimes b\prime\mapsto\ell_i(b)\ell_j(b\prime)$, supplied by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. This extracts exactly the corresponding entry of $T_iT_j-T_jT_i$. Hence $T_iT_j=T_jT_i$ for all $i,j$.

source.place: Remark 4.1, p.84, matrix formula (25), together with Lemma 16.11, p.327; explicit two-universal-points coefficient calculation.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-commuting-endomorphisms-common-eigenvector] to the finite family $(T_i)$: its field is algebraically closed by hypothesis, $V$ is finite-dimensional and nonzero, and step 2 proves all required commutations. Obtain $v\ne0$ with $T_i(v)=\lambda_i v$ for every $i$. Put $L=kv$ and $a=\sum_i\lambda_i c_i\in B$. For every commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and $g\in G(A)$, step 1 now gives $r_A(g)(1\otimes v)=f_g(a)(1\otimes v)$. By $A$-linearity this preserves $A\otimes_k L$, and $\dim_kL=1$.

source.place: Lemma 16.11, p.327; Definition 16.1, p.324, applied to the universal coefficient operators rather than only rational points.

proof.text: Choose a basis of $V$ beginning with $v$. In this basis the universal matrix has first column $(a,0,\ldots,0)^t$. Applying the same stable-line formula to $u^{-1}\in G(B)$ shows that its inverse has first column $(b,0,\ldots,0)^t$ for some $b\in B$. Multiplying gives $ab=1$, so $a$ is a unit. Consequently the regular-function map $k[t,t^{-1}]\to B$, $t\mapsto a$, $t^{-1}\mapsto b$, defines a scheme morphism $\chi:G\to\mathbf G_m=\operatorname{GL}_1$ by [def-weil-affine-spectrum] and [def-sc-general-linear-group]. For any $A,g$, its value is $\chi_A(g)=f_g(a)\in A^\times$.

source.place: Remark 4.1, p.84; characters and eigenspaces, section 4(g), pp.91–92; explicit rank-one matrix construction.

proof.text: For any $A$ and $g,h\in G(A)$, applying $r_A(gh)=r_A(g)r_A(h)$ to $1\otimes v$ gives $\chi_A(gh)=\chi_A(g)\chi_A(h)$: equality of coefficients follows because $1\otimes v$ is a member of a basis of $A\otimes_kV$. The identity matrix similarly gives $\chi_A(1)=1$. Thus $\chi$ is a group-scheme homomorphism by the functor-of-points formulation of [def-sc-group-scheme]. The formula of step 3 extends to every $w\in L$ by $k$-linearity and is exactly the required character formula. All calculations were over arbitrary algebras, so neither reducedness nor smoothness nor connectedness was used.

source.place: Definition 16.1, p.324; section 4(g), pp.91–92, character action formula; conclusion of Corollary 16.14, p.329.

proof_origin.place: Explicit coefficient-matrix proof of Corollary 16.14 using Remark 4.1 and Lemma 16.11; avoids the smoothness hypothesis of Proposition 16.12 and the structural classification in Theorem 16.13.
